issues.legal_issue: A mining-lease recommendation is invalid when the authority selects applicants using past investments and applicant categories instead of applying the governing statutory criteria.
material_facts: The State considered applications from 111 applicants for mining leases over a notified area.
The Chief Minister’s proceedings divided applicants into groups and ultimately preferred companies with existing steel-plant investments, including the selected applicants.
The proceedings did not adequately assess the statutory factors for comparing applicants, and gave no clear reasons for preferring the selected applicants over others.
issues.conclusion: The State’s recommendation was contrary to the statutory scheme and could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2 and 11(3)–(5) of the MMDR Act and the Mineral Concession Rules form the governing scheme; the State acts as a delegate and must exercise its power in the manner prescribed by that scheme. It cannot rely on criteria outside the Act and Rules or frame a policy de hors them. The Court relied on State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar, State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd., Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. State of Bihar, State of Assam v. Om Prakash Mehta, Quarry Owners’ Association v. State of Bihar, C.I.T. Mumbai v. Anjum M.H. Ghaswala, Captain Sube Singh v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, and State of U.P. v. Singhara Singh.

rule.if: mining_lease_allocation and applications_evaluated_in_stages and selection_based_on_past_plant_investment and statutory_merits_not_assessed

predicates.mining_lease_allocation: The authority considered competing applications for mining leases over an area.
predicates.applications_evaluated_in_stages: The authority divided the applicants into categories and evaluated those categories in successive stages.
predicates.selection_based_on_past_plant_investment: The authority preferred applicants because they had already invested in plants based on the mineral.
predicates.statutory_merits_not_assessed: The authority did not adequately assess the applicants using the governing statutory merits criteria.

issues.definition: When a mining-lease allocation is conducted through staged categories, preference rests on past plant investment, and statutory merits are not adequately assessed, the recommendation is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An application filed before public notification of a previously held area cannot be entertained alongside applications filed in response to that notification.
material_facts: The area sought had previously been held under a mining lease and was later notified as available for regrant.
One applicant had applied for a lease before the notification but did not apply in response to it.
Other applicants applied after the notification.
issues.conclusion: The pre-notification application was premature and could not be entertained with the applications made in response to the notification.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(4) of the MMDR Act governs applications for notified areas covered by Rule 59(1); only applications made pursuant to the notification are considered together. Rules 59 and 60 require notification before a previously held area becomes available and provide that premature applications shall not be entertained. The first proviso to Section 11(2) concerns virgin areas, not areas governed by Rule 59. The Court relied on Amritlal Nathubhai Shah v. Union Government of India, State of Tamil Nadu v. M.S. Hindstone, State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya, and Gujarat Pradesh Panchayat Parishad v. State of Gujarat.

rule.if: mining_lease_grant_proceeding and previously_held_area and public_notification_required and application_preceded_notification

predicates.mining_lease_grant_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an application for grant of a mining lease.
predicates.previously_held_area: The area had previously been held under a mining lease or otherwise falls within a category requiring public notice before regrant.
predicates.public_notification_required: The area could not be granted until its availability had been publicly notified.
predicates.application_preceded_notification: The applicant filed the grant application before the public notification.

issues.definition: In a mining-lease grant proceeding for an area requiring public notification, an application filed before that notification must not be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A direction to consider applications in accordance with law does not authorize consideration of applications filed before the notification opening a previously held area for grant.
material_facts: An earlier court order directed consideration of applications in accordance with the governing law and referred to applications made pursuant to the notification.
The order did not direct the authority to consider all applications filed before the notification.
The applicant whose application predated the notification relied on that order to support consideration of its application.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order did not permit consideration of the pre-notification application.
issues.legal_principle: A court direction to consider applications in accordance with the MMDR Act and the Mineral Concession Rules does not displace the limits imposed by Section 11 and Rules 59 and 60. The order at issue had not decided the interpretation of those provisions and contained no mandamus requiring consideration of prior applications.

predicates.mining_lease_allocation: The proceeding concerns competing applications for a mining lease.
predicates.earlier_order_requires_lawful_considerat: An earlier court order directed the authority to consider applications in accordance with law.
predicates.earlier_order_does_not_direct_considerat: The earlier order did not expressly direct consideration of applications filed before the relevant notification.
predicates.application_preceded_notification: The application relied on was filed before the notification opening the area for grant.

issues.definition: Where an earlier order requires lawful consideration but does not direct consideration of prior applications, it does not authorize consideration of an application filed before the notification.

issues.legal_issue: The end-use factor in the preferential-right rule did not justify preferring applicants who shared the same intended use in a notified-area allocation.
material_facts: The State relied on the end-use rule to support its preference for selected applicants with existing investments in steel plants.
All the competing applicants, including the selected applicants and the excluded applicants, proposed to use the iron ore to produce steel.
The applications concerned an area opened for grant by notification.
issues.conclusion: The end-use rule did not justify the State’s preference in this allocation; it permits consideration of different end uses and applies to cases under Section 11(2), not the notified-area process under Section 11(4).
issues.legal_principle: Rule 35 adds the end use of the mineral to the factors in Section 11(3) for purposes of Section 11(2). It permits comparison of different end uses, but does not distinguish applicants who propose the same end use. The Court also held that Rule 35 does not govern applications considered under Section 11(4).

predicates.notified_area_mining_lease_allocation: The authority considered competing mining-lease applications for an area opened for grant by public notification.
predicates.competing_applicants_share_same_end_use: The competing applicants proposed the same use for the mineral.
predicates.authority_relied_on_end_use_to_prefer_so: The authority invoked the applicants’ intended use of the mineral to justify preferring some over others.

issues.definition: In a notified-area allocation, when competing applicants propose the same end use, that shared end use does not support preferring some applicants.

issues.legal_issue: Past investment and captive consumption in existing plants cannot substitute for proposed investment as a basis for preferring an applicant in an initial grant of a mining lease.
material_facts: The State preferred applicants because they had already established steel plants and sought ore for captive consumption and value addition.
The grant at issue was an initial grant, not a renewal of an existing lease.
The applicants proposed to use the mineral in the steel industry, but the State relied on their past investments rather than assessing proposed investment under the statutory criteria.
issues.conclusion: Past investments and captive consumption in existing plants were not valid grounds for the preference given in this initial grant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(3)(d) refers to investment an applicant proposes to make, not past investment. Rule 35 concerns end use, not the extent of an applicant’s existing investment, and does not expand the proposed-investment factor. TISCO v. Union of India concerned a second renewal under Section 8(3), where the broad criterion of mineral development permitted consideration of captive consumption; it did not govern an initial grant under Section 11. Indian Charge Chrome Ltd. v. Union of India also held that captive mining cannot be the controlling factor for a grant.

predicates.initial_mining_lease_grant: The proceeding concerns an initial grant of a mining lease rather than renewal of an existing lease.
predicates.preference_based_on_existing_plant_or_ca: The authority preferred an applicant because of an existing plant or a need to consume the mineral captively.
predicates.proposed_investment_not_the_basis: The preference was not based on the investment the applicant proposed to make in the mine and related industry.

issues.definition: For an initial mining-lease grant, preference based on an existing plant or captive use cannot replace assessment of proposed investment.

issues.legal_issue: Past commitments by the State to an applicant cannot justify a mining-lease grant contrary to the governing statutory criteria.
material_facts: The selected applicants relied on alleged State commitments connected with their existing steel plants and need for iron ore.
The State had notified the area for grant and considered competing applications.
The statutory scheme supplied the criteria for deciding among those applications.
issues.conclusion: Any past commitments by the State were irrelevant to the grant and could not justify preferring the selected applicants.
issues.legal_principle: The MMDR Act and Mineral Concession Rules constitute the governing scheme for mining-lease grants, and the State cannot act inconsistently with that scheme or make commitments that displace its criteria. The Court relied on State of Assam v. Om Prakash Mehta, Quarry Owners’ Association v. State of Bihar, M.A. Tulloch, Baijnath Kedia, Kesoram Industries, Bharat Coking Coal, Anjum M.H. Ghaswala, Captain Sube Singh, and Singhara Singh.

predicates.mining_lease_grant_under_statutory_schem: The proceeding concerns a mining-lease grant governed by a statutory allocation scheme.
predicates.authority_relied_on_past_state_commitmen: The authority relied on an earlier State commitment to justify preferring an applicant.

issues.definition: When a mining-lease grant is governed by a statutory scheme, a past State commitment cannot serve as a ground for preferring an applicant.

issues.legal_issue: Equitable considerations cannot preserve a mining-lease recommendation that violates the governing statute.
material_facts: The recommendation in favour of the selected applicants was made under a statutory scheme governing mining-lease grants.
The recommendation was inconsistent with the scheme’s requirements and criteria.
The selected applicants relied on equitable considerations, including commitments and existing investments.
issues.conclusion: Equity could not save the recommendation because the field was governed by statute and the recommendation violated that statute.
issues.legal_principle: Equity is excluded where a matter is governed by statute and cannot validate action contrary to statutory requirements. The Court relied on Kedar Lal v. Hari Lal Sea and Raja Ram v. Aba Maruti Mali.

predicates.statutory_scheme_governs_mining_lease_gr: A statutory scheme governs the grant of the mining lease.
predicates.recommendation_conflicts_with_statutory_: The recommendation was made contrary to the requirements of that scheme.
predicates.equitable_relief_invoked: A party relied on equitable considerations to preserve the recommendation.

issues.definition: When a statutory scheme governs a mining-lease grant and the recommendation conflicts with it, equitable considerations cannot validate the recommendation.

issues.legal_issue: An approval based on an invalid State recommendation cannot stand, and the matter should not be remitted to the approving authority to reconsider that same recommendation.
material_facts: The Central Government approved the proposed grants after the State had forwarded its recommendation.
The Central Government considered the materials sent with that recommendation rather than independently assessing all applicants’ merits.
The State recommendation was invalid, and sending the matter back to the Central Government risked a post-decisional process influenced by the judgment upholding the grants.
The Court considered that the Central Government’s approval function did not provide an independent process for comparing all applicants and hearing their claims.
issues.conclusion: The consequential Central Government approval could not stand, and the Court rejected the request to remit the matter to the Central Government.
issues.legal_principle: A defective State recommendation cannot support a valid consequential approval. The Court relied on Barnard v. National Dock Labour Board, McFoy v. United Africa Co., Pavani Sridhara Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, State of Kerala v. Puthenkavu N.S.S. Karayogam, H.L. Trehan v. Union of India, K.I. Shephard v. Union of India, Shekhar Ghosh v. Union of India, Union of India v. R. Gandhi, and Indian Charge Chrome Ltd. v. Union of India. It held that the approval function was not a substitute for the State’s consideration of all applications and that a remittal in the circumstances would risk an impermissible post-decisional hearing.

predicates.challenge_to_mining_lease_approval: The proceeding challenges an approval of a proposed mining-lease grant.
predicates.state_recommendation_invalid: The State recommendation supporting the proposed grant was invalid.
predicates.central_approval_based_on_state_recommen: The approving authority relied on the State recommendation and the materials sent with it.
predicates.central_authority_did_not_independently_: The approving authority did not independently assess and compare all applicants on their merits.

issues.definition: When a challenged mining-lease approval rests on an invalid State recommendation and the approving authority did not independently assess all applicants, the approval cannot stand and remittal to that authority is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: Quashing an entire availability notification is unwarranted when the defect lies in the later recommendation and the notification itself is not the relief properly at issue.
material_facts: The single Judge quashed the State’s recommendation and also quashed the notification that had invited applications for the area.
The single Judge thereby went beyond the relief sought in the writ petitions.
The Supreme Court upheld the quashing of the recommendation but deleted the additional directions and observations concerning the notification.
issues.conclusion: The quashing of the notification was set aside, while the quashing of the recommendation was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Relief must be confined to the defect established and the relief sought. The defect in the consideration and recommendation did not warrant quashing the notification that opened the area for applications.

rule.if: challenge_directed_at_later_lease_recommendation and notification_invited_public_applications and defect_lies_in_recommendation and notification_not_shown_defective

predicates.challenge_directed_at_later_lease_recomm: The proceeding challenged a recommendation made after applications had been invited.
predicates.notification_invited_public_applications: The notification opened the area for applications from the public.
predicates.defect_lies_in_recommendation: The established defect concerned the authority’s later consideration or recommendation.
predicates.notification_not_shown_defective: The notification itself was not shown to be defective.

issues.definition: If the defect lies in the later recommendation rather than the public notification, the notification should not be quashed.

issues.legal_issue: When a State recommendation is invalid, the State must reconsider all applications under the governing statutory criteria without the reviewing court deciding the applicants’ comparative merits.
material_facts: The State’s recommendation was invalid under the statutory scheme.
The Court concluded that it had not determined the eligibility or comparative merits of any applicant.
The State had considered applications for the notified area and could reconsider them in light of the Court’s interpretation of the governing provisions.
issues.conclusion: The State was directed to consider all applications afresh and make a new recommendation in accordance with law; the Court expressed no view on the applicants’ eligibility or merits.
issues.legal_principle: The State must apply Section 11 of the MMDR Act and Rules 35, 59, and 60 of the Mineral Concession Rules when reconsidering the applications. The Court’s ruling concerned the interpretation of those provisions and did not determine any applicant’s eligibility or comparative merits.

predicates.state_mining_lease_recommendation_invali: The State’s recommendation on competing mining-lease applications was invalid.
predicates.competing_applications_remain_undecided: The applications remain pending for a lawful decision on their merits.
predicates.reviewing_court_has_not_resolved_applica: The reviewing court has not decided the applicants’ eligibility or comparative merits.

issues.definition: When an invalid recommendation leaves competing applications undecided and the reviewing court has not resolved their merits, the State must reconsider all applications under the governing law.
